Article Title: Brics embraces AI but leaves job displacement largely unaddressed
Article Text:
Brics New Delhi Declaration backs AI-driven growth and worker re-skilling but leaves unanswered what happens to jobs lost to automation.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Brics has set out an ambitious plan to prepare people for an AI-driven economy, but its New Delhi Declaration leaves a key question largely unanswered — what happens to workers whose jobs are lost or sharply changed because of automation and AI?The declaration calls AI an “immense opportunity to stimulate economic growth and sustainable development for all” and backs wider access to AI, while stressing safety, security, inclusion and reliability. But on employment, its response is largely to prepare workers for changing skill needs rather than spell out what happens when technology replaces existing work.The declaration commits Brics countries to strengthen cooperation in “forecasting skills needs by analysing labour market trends in digital, green, care and other priority sectors”. It also welcomes Brics Connect, the “BRICS Cooperation Network for Capacity Building, Employability, and New Skills and Technologies”, focused on skills for changing labour markets.The declaration addresses some changes already taking place. It calls for nationally tailored approaches to expand social protection for gig and platform workers and recognises the need to protect workers moving across borders, including through portability of benefits. It also notes an initiative to establish an “International Digital Platform for Remote Employment” for Brics countries.But there is no equivalent, specific commitment on workers whose existing jobs may disappear because of AI.The declaration does not propose a Brics system to identify occupations exposed to automation, provide transition support to affected workers or measure AI-related job losses.That gap stands out because Brics is simultaneously encouraging wider use of AI across its economies. Its Centre for Industrial Competencies supports manufacturing companies, including SMEs, in adopting Industry 4.0 and advanced digital production technologies, including AI.Brics does recognise some AI-related risks beyond employment. In the intellectual property section, it notes “risks relating to misappropriation and misrepresentation of knowledge, heritage, and cultural values” that are insufficiently represented in datasets and AI models.For workers the declaration promises labour markets that are “future-ready”, “ensuring that no worker is left behind”.
Article Summary: Brics new delhi declaration backs ai-driven growth and worker re-skilling. But it leaves unanswered what happens to jobs lost to automation. Declaration does not propose a brics system to identify occupations exposed to automation, provide transition support to affected workers or measure ai-related job losses.

NEW DELHI: Commerce and industry minister Piyush Goyal Friday called for dismantling of trade barriers by Brics nations while urging them to link payment systems and trade in each other's local currency."We should open our markets for each other's products, including raw material and critical minerals. Our supply chains will be resilient when they run both ways, with non-tariff measures imposing higher import costs, in fact much more than the tariffs themselves," the minister said at Brics Business Forum.He called for streamlining regulatory and customs processes while also promoting services trade. "Let us open our services market for each other in the real sense, let professionals move easily across borders and make it easier to recognise each other's professional qualifications," the minister said.The comments come amid several countries holding up visas for Indian professionals and some like China mounting curbs on the export of many items while denying market access to goods from parts of the world.Pointing to initiatives taken by govt in laying out digital public infrastructure, Goyal said, "Today, it (UPI) is also accepted in 11 countries and I would urge Brics member countries and partner countries to link our payment systems, trade in each other's local currencies, make digital trade global and build together for the future emerging technologies."External affairs minister S Jaishankar called upon member nations to work towards addressing economic challenges by ensuring transparent trade and investment practices. "The common thread is how to make it easier for businesses in our countries to find more partners, access more markets, connect supply networks and convert complementarities into viable commercial partnerships," the EAM said, while pointing to geopolitical tensions.

Article Title: FSSAI orders recall of two food products
Article Text:
Representative image

NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India ( FSSAI ) has ordered recall of two food products after testing found them non-compliant with standards.Recall orders pertain to "Shalimar's Chef - Coriander Powder" manufactured by M/s Nilgiri Oil & Allied Industries and "Carrageenan" manufactured by M/s Aquagri Processing Pvt Ltd. A sample of coriander powder was found unsatisfactory with respect to pesticide residues. After retesting, the sample was found non-compliant and opined to be "unsafe" under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.The Carrageenan sample was found unsatisfactory with respect to food additives and did not conform to standards. The referral food lab opined that the sample was "unsafe". Both operators have been directed to recall products from market in accordance with Food Safety and Standards (Food Recall Procedure) Regulations, 2017. TNN

Article Title: Global nutrition experts back FSSAI warning labels, seek stricter rules
Article Text:
FSSAI

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Over 60 nutrition and public health scholars from 17 countries, including researchers from Harvard, Johns Hopkins and Oxford, have backed India's mandatory warning labels on packaged foods and beverages high in nutrients of health concern, while urging FSSAI to strengthen system.In a written comment to Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, the scholars called for removal of the proposed "two or more nutrients" requirement, saying products high in one nutrient of concern should carry a warning. They said sugar, saturated fat and sodium can pose health risks and cited WHO guidance supporting thresholds.The intervention comes amid the debate over front-of-package labelling. Supreme Court has also questioned FSSAI's proposed phased rollout, including its "two or more nutrients" threshold, and sought a timeline for implementing front-of-package warnings.Dr Arun Gupta, founder of Breastfeeding Promotion Network of India and convenor of Nutrition Advocacy for Public Interest, said the scholars' recommendations counter position taken by All India Food Processors Association, which opposed warning labels and advocated per-serving labelling.The scholars said warning labels have evidence of changing consumer behaviour, improving nutritional profile of the food supply and making purchases and dietary intake healthier. They cited evidence of reductions in calories, sugar, saturated fat and sodium.
Article Summary: Over 60 nutrition and public health scholars from 17 countries have backed india's mandatory warning labels on packaged foods and beverages. The intervention comes amid the debate over front-of-package labelling. Supreme court has also questioned fssai's proposed phased rollout, including its "two or more nutrients" threshold.

Article Title: Bid to boost education, employability
Article Text:
Brics Summit 2026

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Brics countries want to bring education and jobs closer together, with a new focus on STEM, vocational training, digital skills and AI, while also trying to identify what skills employers will need in the coming years.The New Delhi Declaration links the entire chain — from basic learning and digital literacy to higher education, technical training and jobs. It calls for cooperation in foundational literacy, digital literacy, and safe and human-centred use of emerging technologies, including AI. It also backs undergraduate and postgraduate scholarships in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM), and stronger links between technical and vocational education and training (TVET) institutions and industry to “expand job opportunities”.A key part of the plan is to make training respond more closely to changes in the job market. Brics members have committed to studying labour-market trends in digital, green, care and other priority sectors to forecast the skills that will be needed. The declaration also welcomes Brics Connect, a network focused on capacity building, employability and new skills and technologies.The emphasis is not only on university education. The declaration recognises Brics TVET Cooperation Alliance as a platform for sharing information and resources and developing vocational training across member countries.It calls for training programmes to be aligned with changing market needs by building stronger links between TVET institutions and industry.The industrial sector is being brought into this effort too. Brics Centre for Industrial Competencies, set up with UNIDO, is helping manufacturers and small businesses adopt Industry 4.0 and advanced digital production technologies, including AI. Brics Intelligent Manufacturing and Robotics Working Group is also working on talent development.The declaration separately calls for greater cooperation in digital skills and capacity building, including proposed capacity-building centres aimed at creating a “future-ready workforce”.For Brics, therefore, the skills challenge is no longer confined to colleges and training centres. The declaration seeks to connect what students learn with what factories, businesses and other employers will need — while using labour-market trends to keep training relevant as technology changes.
Article Summary: The new delhi declaration links the entire chain — from basic learning and digital literacy to higher education, technical training and jobs. It calls for cooperation in foundational literacy, digital literacy, and safe and human-centred use of emerging technologies, including ai.

Article Title: Silver prices crash over 40% from Rs 4 lakh/kg high to Rs 2.35 lakh, but buyers are still staying away; bigger problem yet to arrive as 2,000 tonnes ordered by Indian dealers risk piling up
Article Text:
Traders and analysts have said that the slowdown in investment demand can be seen across silver exchange-traded funds (ETFs), bars and coins.

Silver Demand Weakens

Massive stockpiling of silver

Silver’s Spectacular Fall

(Disclaimer: Recommendations and views on the stock market, or any other asset classes or personal finance management tips given by experts and analysts are their own. These opinions do not represent the views of The Times of India.)

A huge crash in silver prices should have led to a revival in demand, but investors seem to be staying away. And this has raised a fresh worry ahead of the festive season.Silver refiners and bullion dealers are seeing their inventories build up as new investment demand for the metal weakens. The situation comes even as silver prices have dropped by more than 40% from their January peak of over Rs 4 lakh per kg. Uncertainty over a possible breakthrough in the US-Iran war and concerns about subdued industrial demand have added to the pressure.In Mumbai’s spot market, silver was trading at Rs 2.35 lakh per kg earlier this week.Traders and analysts have said that the slowdown in investment demand can be seen across silver exchange-traded funds (ETFs), bars and coins. Investors who bought the metal when prices were significantly higher are now sitting on substantial losses, making them hesitant to make fresh purchases despite the steep correction in prices!Also Read | A couple sold gold for Rs 20 lakh to buy a home, another family got Rs 80 lakh for a US degree and business: How Indians are unlocking value of idle gold sitting in their lockers "Investment demand for silver ETFs, bars and coins has come down. Internationally, prices are unlikely to cross $100 per troy ounce immediately unless the US-Iran war comes to an end. Silver prices are undervalued," Chirag Sheth, global business head, Public Gold Bullion (SG) Pte told ET. "The continuous war between US and Iran has impacted the solar industry, semiconductor industry and EV industry where silver is used. "The weak demand is also creating an inventory problem for domestic players.Indian bullion dealers and refiners have reportedly placed orders for around 2,000 tonnes of silver, which is currently in transit. The additional supplies have raised concerns over a further build-up in stocks. India imports around 7,000 tonnes of silver every year."With no new investors coming in and no immediate signs of prices going up, refiners and bullion dealers are facing a problem internationally as well as in domestic markets," said James Jose, president, Precious Metals Refiners Forum.Silver prices have fallen steadily over the past seven months, following an extraordinary rally that pushed the metal more than 300% higher year-on-year. In January, silver crossed Rs 4 lakh per kg on the Multi Commodity Exchange for the first time."The market is still digesting the aftermath of the speculation-driven frenzy, and this may be prompting investors to stay away after many of them incurred significant losses," said Carsten Menke, head, Next Generation Research, Julius Baer told ET.The outlook for industrial demand is adding to the pressure, with consumption expected to weaken. "A shift to cheaper alternatives, such as aluminium and copper, has started, and the growth outlook for Chinese solar module makers, which are the biggest industrial users of silver, is not as strong anymore," Menke said.The ongoing US-Iran war has added to the negative sentiment surrounding silver. If the conflict continues for an extended period, investors may remain cautious. At the same time, expectations of weaker industrial consumption could make a rapid rebound in silver prices difficult.Despite the sharp fall, some long-term investors are once again looking at silver as a way to diversify their portfolios."The market has taken full cognisance of the marked decline in silver prices in recent days. Some investors have shaved off their allocation, while others have prepared for fresh acquisition depending on their views and goals," said Nilanjan Dey, partner, Wishlist Capital.Dey said investors who have a time horizon of five years or longer may look at buying silver ETFs in a staggered manner instead of putting in a large amount at one go. Monthly or fortnightly investments could help spread out the purchase price and reduce the impact of short-term price movements.For first-time investors looking to add precious metals to their portfolios as a diversification from equities, ETFs can provide exposure without the need to hold or manage physical silver. However, Dey warned that investors with a shorter investment horizon should not assume that the recent decline automatically makes silver an attractive buying opportunity.
Article Summary: Silver refiners and bullion dealers are seeing their inventories build up as new investment demand for the metal weakens. Investors who bought the metal when prices were significantly higher are now sitting on substantial losses. Uncertainty over a possible breakthrough in the us-iran war and concerns about subdued industrial demand have added to the pressure.

Article Title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max get Variable Aperture as 'most important' camera feature: What it means for users
Article Text:
Apple iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max

Aperture is the part of a camera most phone users never see

The useful bit is what happens when you take control

It is not just about low light

The aperture is only on one camera

Apple is adding more control to video too

The idea isn't new to smartphones

The bigger camera change is the combination

What variable aperture actually changes for iPhone users

Apple has added variable aperture to the main camera on both the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. This will offer users a physical way to control how much light reaches the sensor for the first time on an iPhone.The feature sits alongside a new 48MP Fusion Main camera, a redesigned sensor and new Pro Controls. Apple says the six laser-cut blades inside the lens can move between four aperture settings, while the camera can also adjust the aperture automatically depending on the scene.That sounds like a minor hardware upgrade. But it is not. The lens opening affects exposure, depth of field, and how motion is captured, so giving the iPhone aperture control adds something software alone can't quite duplicate.Apple's description is straightforward: "iPhone 18 Pro has a new 48 megapixel fusion main camera with variable aperture for creative control that wasn't possible before," Apple said. "This is the most advanced camera we've ever made."Aperture is simply the opening through which light passes before reaching a camera's image sensor. It is measured using f-numbers such as f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8 and f/4.0.The lower the f-number, the wider the opening and the more light reaches the sensor.A wider aperture can therefore help in darker conditions. A narrower aperture lets in less light, but it also keeps more of the scene in focus.Most smartphone cameras use a fixed aperture. The lens has one opening, and the phone relies heavily on shutter speed, ISO, and computational photography to handle different lighting conditions.The iPhone 18 Pro changes that for its main camera. Its lens can open as wide as f/1.48 and then stop down to f/1.8, f/2.8 or f/4.0. Six blades inside the lens physically change the opening size.Apple says the blades are laser-cut and thinner than a human hair. They are designed to move smoothly between the available settings rather than simply switching between two fixed positions.The camera can make that decision automatically. In a darker scene, it can open the aperture to f/1.48 and let in more light. In brighter conditions, it can narrow the opening.For most people, the automatic system will do most of the work. The Camera app can choose an aperture based on the scene, just as it already decides on exposure and other settings.The difference is that iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max owners can also take control themselves.Apple's new Pro Controls let users manually change aperture, shutter speed, and white balance. A histogram can also be displayed to help judge exposure across a scene.That gives photographers another way to decide how a picture should look, instead of leaving every exposure decision to the camera.The most obvious example is depth of field. At a wider aperture such as f/1.48, the camera can produce more optical background blur when the subject is relatively close and the background is farther away.Stopping down to f/4.0 has the opposite effect. More of the scene can stay in focus, which can help with landscapes or group photos where people stand at different distances from the camera.That matters because a group shot can otherwise leave one person sharp while another, standing slightly farther away, falls outside the plane of focus. A narrower aperture gives the camera more room to keep those subjects in focus.It also gives photographers another option when deliberately introducing motion into an image. A narrower aperture reduces the amount of light entering the lens, making it easier to use a slower shutter speed when conditions are bright enough.The obvious benefit of opening the aperture is light. Apple says the main camera can open to ƒ/1.48 for low-light photography, letting more light reach the sensor.That can give the camera more flexibility before it has to compensate by increasing ISO or slowing the shutter speed. In practical terms, that can help preserve detail and reduce noise, while a fast enough shutter can keep moving subjects sharp.But variable aperture is useful in the opposite direction too.In bright daylight, photographers sometimes want a slower shutter speed to create motion blur. That can be useful with moving water, people, or cars, and it also matters in video, where shutter speed is normally tied to frame rate.A fixed wide aperture can make that difficult in strong sunlight because too much light reaches the sensor even when the shutter is already operating at its fastest useful setting. Stopping the lens down gives the camera another way to reduce exposure.There are limits, though. A range ending at f/4.0 does not eliminate the need for neutral-density filters in every bright-light situation. Photographers who want long exposures in direct sunlight may still need an ND filter to cut the light further.Apple's implementation has an important limitation. The variable aperture is on the main 24mm camera. It does not extend across the entire rear camera system.The ultra-wide and telephoto cameras don't have the same variable-aperture mechanism. That means the new optical control is available only when shooting through the main lens.This is also why the feature should not be viewed as a replacement for the other cameras or for computational photography. Exposure, autofocus, HDR, noise reduction and image processing still determine much of the final photograph.The hardware simply gives the camera another physical variable to work with before those processes take over.Aperture changes also feed into Apple's video features. The new Pro Controls work with video as well as photography, letting users manually adjust settings including aperture and shutter speed. That is especially relevant for people who want more predictable exposure rather than letting the phone change settings during recording.Apple has also added the ability to apply Cinematic effects after capture to videos recorded at up to 60 frames per second. That means users can make this adjustment after recording instead of committing to the effect while shooting.Time-lapse recording now supports 4K and Dolby Vision HDR, while Audio Mix has new algorithms designed to improve voice quality and isolate music.The combination is notable because Apple isn't presenting the variable aperture as an isolated camera specification. It is part of a broader attempt to give users more control over how photos and video are captured and processed.Apple is not the first phone maker to put a variable aperture in a smartphone. Samsung introduced a dual-aperture system with the Galaxy S9 series in 2018. That system switched between f/1.5 and f/2.4 depending on the lighting conditions.Huawei later introduced more flexible variable-aperture systems, while Xiaomi and Honor have also used the technology in flagship phones.The reason it has remained relatively uncommon is fairly simple: fitting a mechanical aperture mechanism into a smartphone camera adds complexity to an already tightly packed module.For years, phone makers instead concentrated on larger sensors, multiple cameras and computational photography. Those technologies can compensate for many of the limitations of a fixed aperture without adding moving parts to the lens.The iPhone 18 Pro's approach is therefore less about replacing computational photography than adding an optical control alongside it.The variable aperture gets most of the attention, but Apple has made several other changes to the camera system.The 48MP Fusion Main camera uses a new sensor and a new computational imaging pipeline that Apple says produces sharper, more detailed images. Photographic Styles now include additional texture and grain controls, giving users more ways to change the look of their photos.Apple has also added persistent subject tracking for photos and video, letting the camera keep following a person even if they temporarily disappear behind someone else in a crowd.Another feature aimed at photographers is Apple Reference Image. When Reference mode is used, the camera captures signed sensor data that Private Cloud Compute turns into what Apple describes as an "unalterable reference image." You can then view the reference alongside the main photograph in the Photos app.The idea is to compare the original sensor-derived reference with the photograph and identify whether changes have been made. Apple says the feature is intended to address image authenticity, particularly for photographers and photojournalists.Apple is also adding metadata support and upcoming support for the SynthID standard to help identify images generated or edited with AI.For someone who simply opens the Camera app and takes pictures, it may not change much. The phone can choose the aperture automatically, just as it already handles most exposure decisions. For people who shoot deliberately, the change is more useful.A wider f/1.48 setting can help in darker scenes. Stopping down can keep more of a group or landscape in focus. Manual aperture control can also be combined with shutter-speed control to create particular motion effects.It can even produce optical effects that fixed-aperture smartphone cameras cannot reproduce in the same way, including changes in how bright points of light appear at narrower apertures.But four aperture settings don't turn the iPhone into a dedicated interchangeable-lens camera. The sensor remains small compared with most conventional cameras, and the amount of natural optical background blur depends heavily on the distance between the camera, subject, and background.For many portraits, Apple's computational Portrait mode will still produce a stronger and more controllable background-blur effect.The same is true for long exposures in bright daylight. The f/1.48-to-f/4.0 range gives photographers more room, but it does not remove the physical limits imposed by available light.That is probably the right way to look at the iPhone 18 Pro's variable aperture. It gives the camera one more physical control over exposure and focus, while the sensor and software continue to determine what ultimately reaches the screen.For casual users, most of that will happen automatically. For photographers and videographers who want to decide how the shot is captured, the four aperture settings and Pro Controls make the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max considerably more flexible than a fixed-aperture iPhone.
Article Summary: Aperture is the opening through which light passes before reaching a camera's image sensor. Six blades inside the lens physically change the opening size. Apple says the blades are laser-cut and thinner than a human hair. They are designed to move smoothly between the available settings.

Article Title: ARC raises Rs 10.5 crore in pre-seed funding
Article Text: ARC, a gaming technology company has raised Rs 10.5 crore in pre‑seed funding led by Chimera VC and MIXI Global Investments, with participation from Dhruv Vohra, Director, Meta, APAC, in his personal capacity. The funding will accelerate development and commercialisation of ARC X1, covering hardware engineering, product validation, manufacturing readiness, and further development of OWL OS and ARC’s gaming software platform. It will also support team expansion, go‑to‑market capabilities, and strategic partnerships across gaming, cloud, content and technology.The global portable gaming console market was valued at US$3.89 billion in 2025 and is projected to grow at 9.7% CAGR through 2033. ARC aims to tap into India’s large mobile‑first gaming community and the low penetration of dedicated gaming hardware, creating space for a more accessible portable gaming category.Founded by Jobin Joseph and Kaustubh K. Jadhav, ARC is building a platform that integrates hardware, software and gaming experiences. The ARC X1 is a portable gaming system designed to make dedicated gaming more accessible to Indian gamers.ARC is developing its own hardware and software stack, aiming to build an ecosystem across devices, operating systems, software services and gaming experiences.Joseph said the funding will deepen ARC’s technology, accelerate product development and move the company closer to launch. Jadhav added that ARC was founded on the belief that access should not determine how deeply someone experiences gaming, and the funding will help bring ARC X1 to gamers at scale.Chimera VC’s Krish Anurag said ARC fits their thesis of backing companies that can become infrastructure for the next chapter of gaming. MIXI Global Investments’ Tomoharu Urabe said ARC X1 can make handheld gaming more accessible for India’s passionate gaming community.ARC X1 is built on ARM architecture, powered by Qualcomm technology, and runs OWL OS, ARC’s proprietary gaming operating system. It supports native Android gaming, PC‑game compatibility through ARC’s software stack, and cloud gaming. ARC has crossed 50,000 waitlist sign‑ups and collaborated with Qualcomm ahead of launch, adopting a community‑led development model involving gamers through early testing and feedback programmes.
Article Summary: Arc, a gaming technology company has raised rs 10.5 crore in pre‑seed funding. The funding will accelerate development and commercialisation of arc x1. Arc aims to tap into india’s large mobile‑first gaming community and the low penetration of dedicated gaming hardware.

Article Title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu warns companies against sharing sensitive data with AI labs: This is quite serious and …
Article Text:
Sridhar Vembu raises AI data security concerns

Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has raised concerns about the growing use of frontier AI models by companies handling sensitive information. Quoting Fields Medalist Terence Tao, Sridhar Vembu shared an X (formerly Twitter) post that said companies with critical know-how, intellectual property and trade secrets should be careful about trusting their information with frontier AI labs. The mathematician warned that AI could change how researchers share ideas. Tao said, "The incentives may now be pointing in the direction of no longer sharing any promising research directions with the broader community, which would reverse centuries of traditions of open science and do serious long-term damage to the future of the field".Sridhar Vembu said companies with valuable intellectual property and trade secrets should be cautious about putting their information into frontier AI systems. "This is quite serious and it is not just mathematicians and scientists," Vembu wrote.He argued that the concern could apply to companies across industries that have sensitive information they do not want to expose outside their organisations.In the post, Vembu also highlighted the pharmaceutical industry as an example. He said major pharma companies already have their own AI models, often based on open-source models, to avoid giving large AI companies information about new drug molecules and processes they are developing."That caution is well warranted," Sridhar Vembu said.Zoho founder says companies should build their own AI models"Your company's know-how belongs in your own AI model," Vembu wrote. He also said that building and running private AI models is becoming easier and cheaper. “Fortunately they are easy to train and becoming cheaper to run too”.
Article Summary: Sridhar vembu raises ai data security concerns over frontier ai. He said companies with critical know-how, intellectual property and trade secrets should be careful about trusting their information with frontier ai labs. The mathematician warned that ai could change how researchers share ideas.

Article Title: Anthropic researcher who quit over AI safety walked away two months before his stock vested; says: I no longer have anything to gain by…
Article Text:
Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic four months in, two months before his equity vested, saying he no longer had anything to gain from the company's valuation.

Anthropic is heading for one of the biggest IPOs ever, and safety is the sales pitch

Coxon says he never saw Anthropic cut corners. He worries the race will force it.

An Anthropic safety lead replied to the resignation thread and agreed with it

An Anthropic researcher who resigned this week over AI safety fears gave up his entire stake in the company to do it, walking out two months before his equity was due to vest.Jacob Coxon, 27, spent three years doing pretraining research at OpenAI before moving to Anthropic in July. He lasted four months. Staff need six for their stock to vest. His resignation post on X on September 9, now past 130 million views, said neither lab is acting responsibly and that both are "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives".Axios first reported the forfeited equity, after Coxon told the outlet on Wednesday that "I no longer have anything to gain by juicing up Anthropic's valuation" and that he left before any of his shares vested. He still holds equity in OpenAI, where his work included GPT-4o.The company is preparing a listing at a reported $2 trillion valuation, built in large part on its reputation as the frontier lab that takes risk seriously. That is what gives the equity detail its weight. Researchers have walked out of rival labs over safety before, usually after their stock vested. Coxon left with nothing, then criticised the valuation he could have profited from.He drew that line carefully in the interview. Anthropic's safety work is sincere, he said, and he has not seen it compromised to outpace competitors. What worries him is pressure over time. Race hard enough and you cut corners, or skip steps in the oversight process. He also described a mood he thinks becomes self-fulfilling, calling it excessive paranoia about OpenAI and about China. Colleagues, he wrote earlier, have started using words like "crunchtime" and "endgame".His most quoted line was about where these decisions are being taken. It is insane, he said, that the work happens on the MacBooks of engineers in San Francisco rather than in a bunker in the desert like the Manhattan Project.Evan Hubinger, who runs alignment stress testing at Anthropic, wrote that he personally puts the odds of AI killing all humans above 10 percent within the decade. He said the company is trying, but has no plan yet for aligning superintelligence and is not clearly on track to find one.Coxon's argument is partly about candour. Executives soften their phrasing for the press, he wrote, then say the same things privately, and the belief that AI could kill everyone by the end of the decade is not a marketing stunt. He also described something that used to be a thought experiment. Models now know when they are being tested, and reason about the fact while it is happening.He pointed to the recent run of cyber incidents at frontier labs, including July's Hugging Face breach, as evidence the risk has left the theoretical stage. Coxon is among more than 1,000 researchers who recently signed a statement calling for governments to coordinate on a way to slow AI development if models start improving on their own. Anthropic has not commented on his departure.
Article Summary: Jacob coxon quit anthropic four months in, two months before his equity vested. He said he no longer had anything to gain from the company's valuation. Anthropic is heading for one of the biggest ipos ever, and safety is the sales pitch.

Article Title: Google unveils five new sustainability initiatives in India
Article Text: Google is expanding its Solar API to cover more than 300 million rooftops in India, enabling faster and more accurate rooftop solar assessments. Installers can now evaluate a home’s solar potential without an on‑site visit, reducing time and cost. Platforms like Solar Ladder and OpenSolar have already integrated Solar API insights to streamline proposal creation and automate manual roof surveys.Google has signed a long‑term agreement with ReNew Power for a 150‑megawatt solar project in Rajasthan. The company will receive environmental attributes from the clean electricity generated, helping address electricity‑related emissions across its value chain. This marks Google’s second Scope 3‑focused solar project in India, bringing total added capacity to 300 MW.Google is partnering with Mitti Labs to help tens of thousands of smallholder rice farmers adopt Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD), a climate‑smart farming method that reduces methane emissions and conserves water. The initiative is expected to generate up to 3 million tonnes of CO₂e in near‑term warming impact (GWP20) and conserve billions of gallons of water.NASA‑enabled satellite verification will support monitoring and farmer adoption.The Google Center for Climate Technology has selected three inaugural projects focused on green workforce training and low‑carbon construction materials. Google is adding two new focus areas—water stewardship and waste & circularity—and is inviting proposals via the Manthan Platform. Selected applicants will receive support to develop scalable, data‑driven environmental solutions.Google has welcomed the first cohort of the DeepMind Accelerator: AI for the Planet, featuring four Indian startups: Terrastack, Varaha Climate, Farmers for Forests, and Climitra Carbon. These companies use AI, Geo‑AI, drones and satellite models to empower farmers, scale agroforestry, restore biodiversity, and convert biomass into biochar.These five initiatives reflect Google’s push to combine AI, research partnerships and local innovation to advance sustainable development and climate resilience across India.

Google is partnering with mitti labs to help tens of thousands of smallholder rice farmers adopt alternate wetting and drying (awd)

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works



Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an ai model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background.

Article Title: AI data centers are causing 'stress' not just to tech companies, but also private insurers
Article Text:
Massive investments, growing risks



Unique challenges for data centre insurance companies

AI data centers are reportedly putting new pressure on the insurance industry. According to a CNBC report, experts warn that the rapid growth of these projects is becoming a “stress test” not just for tech companies, but also for private insurers and lenders. Consulting firm McKinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. As costs rise, tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects. The scale of investments is creating challenges for insurers.“When you put $10 to $20 billion plus in a single location, it creates capacity issues in the marketplace,” said Tom Harper, data center leader at insurance broker Gallagher as quoted in the CNBC report.He added that the sector has been a “real stress test” over the last few years, as insurers struggle to provide coverage for such large and complex projects. While these facilities are seen as high-quality assets, Harper said insuring them has become difficult due to their size and risk concentration.Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Companies including Nvidia, Microsoft and BlackRock have already taken part in large investment deals.Rajat Rana, partner at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, described the scale as unprecedented. “We’re talking about trillions of dollars, and almost going back to the same cycle where there’s almost no transparency about the financing structures — the scale is astronomical,” he said. He added that the boom in AI data centers could be “the largest peacetime investment project in human history.”Experts say the way these projects are financed is adding another layer of risk. Much of the funding is happening through complex and less transparent debt structures. Rana warned that this trend feels like “deja vu,” referring to past financial cycles. He said the lack of transparency could create risks for investors, insurers and pension funds.As stated in the CNBC report, data centers offer unique challenges due to their mix of real estate and advanced technology. Insurers are now designing custom policies to manage these risks. However, challenges remain. Large facilities are often located in areas prone to extreme weather, and they store expensive equipment, sometimes even before installation.Another key concern is the mismatch between the lifespan of data centers and the hardware they use. While data centers can last decades, GPUs — the chips powering AI — typically last around seven years. Rana described this as a “GPU debt treadmill,” saying, “This is almost like a treadmill that these AI data centers are running on.”He explained that companies may need to keep raising debt to upgrade infrastructure as technology evolves.
Article Summary: Private data center deals have crossed $10 billion regularly, with some reaching as high as $40 billion. Mckinsey estimates that global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030. Tech giants are increasingly relying on private equity, private credit and debt to fund these projects.

Article Title: "Trans women are.....": Clavicular’s viral moment with trans women sparks fresh conversation on internet culture
Article Text:
A viral clip featuring Clavicular and trans women is gaining attention for its calm and honest tone. The conversation explores how online language and trends move across communities. Instead of conflict, the exchange highlights shared influence and mutual awareness. Viewers are engaging with its thoughtful nature, as it reflects how internet culture evolves through collaboration rather than ownership.

Clavicular and trans women share a surprising realization about online trends

The video of Clavicular, a short-video producer, is going around the Internet, yet not the reason why. There is no yelling or over-the-top drama. It is a mere, everyday talk that seems almost novel nowadays, in the age of internet, which is overflowing with content. The scene is easy-going, the tone of the narrative is straightforward, and the characters appear more concerned with conversation than combat.The message that is being addressed is the flow of the conversation. It discusses internet culture, the way people communicate with one another and the place of trends. Rather than bringing out a debate, the encounter towards curiosity. It quietly brings attention to something that a lot of people who use the internet notice but don't often say out loud. People in different communities often have a bigger impact on each other than they think.The conversation begins with a confident and lighthearted comment from one of the trans women present. She says, "You know that trans women are like the OG lip masters, right? We are very talented in the program. Like, I do the peptides, I'm on Zeta." Her tone carries a mix of pride and humor, setting a relaxed vibe at the table.Clavicular responds in a way that keeps the mood steady but adds a different angle.He says, "That is funny because you guys were using a lot of the words in like the South Korean subreddits in like 2014." It’s not confrontational. If anything, it feels like an observation. He points to how certain words and ideas may have traveled across different online spaces over time.Another voice joins in and brings the moment full circle. "Guys, we're like the OGs. I saw a couple of posts about that. We're like copying each other." That line hits in a simple but honest way. It reflects something familiar. Online culture is rarely created in isolation. It grows through sharing, borrowing, and sometimes even unknowingly repeating.That's what makes the clip so powerful. It doesn't want to make a point or win an argument. It only shows a group of people talking, listening, and figuring something out together.This moment feels different in a space where viral content often leads to fights. It reminds people that conversations can be calm, thoughtful, and still important. And sometimes, that honest silence is what makes it work.
Article Summary: A viral clip featuring clavicular and trans women is gaining attention for its calm and honest tone. The conversation explores how online language and trends move across communities. Viewers are engaging with its thoughtful nature, as it reflects how internet culture evolves through collaboration.
